# First variation of maximum ordinary simplex depth under weak added laws

Let T be a full-dimensional d-simplex in R^d, d>=1, of volume V.
Let g be its centroid, m=d+1, h=d/(d+1), Gamma=h^d, and let
lambda_0,...,lambda_d be its affine barycentric coordinates.
Their linear parts are denoted l_i. Put

    H_i={x:lambda_i(x)>=1/m},
    kappa=d V h^(d-1).

For t>0 let nu_t be probability measures converging weakly to a
compactly supported probability nu. Assume

    nu{lambda_i=1/m}=0  for every i.                   (1)

The measures nu_t may have atoms and need not have a common compact
support. No rate of weak convergence relative to t is required.
Define the unnormalized ordinary depth and its maximum by

    mu_t=1_T dx+t nu_t,
    A_t(y)=inf_{|u|=1} mu_t{x:u.x>=u.y},
    D_t=max_{y in R^d} A_t(y).

Write p_i=nu(H_i) and pbar=m^(-1) sum_i p_i. Then

    D_t=Gamma V+t pbar+o(t),                          (2)
    D_t/(V+t)=Gamma+(t/V)(pbar-Gamma)+o(t).           (3)

The maximum exists for all sufficiently small t. Moreover EVERY
choice of maximizing point satisfies

    y_t=g+t v_*+o(t),
    l_i(v_*)=(p_i-pbar)/kappa for all i.              (4)

The m right-hand sides sum to zero, so (4) specifies one unique
vector. Equivalently, if v_i are the simplex vertices,

    v_*=(1/kappa) sum_i(p_i-pbar) v_i.

This is an all-direction maximum-depth statement, not only the
first variation of a prescribed finite cap cover.

## 1. The ordinary simplex inputs

Ordinary Grunbaum gives A_0(g)=Gamma V. Its precise equality case
is recorded and used in
candidate e2c55c91458e1e8c, Section 1:
in a simplex, the only equality directions through its centroid
are the d+1 apex-side caps parallel to opposite facets. These are
exactly H_i above. In d=1 they are the two directions of the line.

There is also a direct unique-maximizer proof. For y in T, the
canonical cap lambda_i>=lambda_i(y) has volume

    V(1-lambda_i(y))^d.                               (5)

If y differs from g, at least one lambda_i(y)>1/m, making this
volume strictly below Gamma V. Outside the interior of T a
separating or supporting cap has zero T-volume. Thus g is the
unique maximizer of the unperturbed depth.

The two facts used below are therefore: all centroid caps have
volume at least Gamma V; equality directions form precisely the
finite set of canonical directions. No mixed-integer result is used.

## 2. Attainment and explicit O(t) localization

For a finite measure, y -> mu_t{x:u.x>=u.y} is upper semicontinuous
for every fixed u, because the cap is closed. The infimum over u
is upper semicontinuous as well. On the compact simplex it attains
its maximum.

At g positivity of the added measure gives A_t(g)>=Gamma V. At
every y outside the interior of T a separating/supporting cap
gives A_t(y)<=t. Thus if t<Gamma V, every global maximizer lies
in int T and the compact maximum is the global one. Also

    Gamma V<=D_t<=Gamma V+t.                          (6)

For any maximizer y_t, its canonical cap at i has added mass at
most t. Equations (5)-(6) imply, for all i,

    lambda_i(y_t)<=1-(Gamma-t/V)^(1/d)=1/m+eta_t,
    eta_t=h-(Gamma-t/V)^(1/d)=O(t).                   (7)

Since the barycentric coordinates sum to one, each is also at
least 1/m-d eta_t. For example, when t<=Gamma V/2,

    eta_t <= t/[d V (Gamma/2)^((d-1)/d)].             (8)

The barycentric affine isomorphism now gives |y_t-g|=O(t),
uniformly over all maximizers. This bound does not use any
regularity or rate assumption on nu_t.

## 3. Weak limits on moving caps and local cap smoothness

We will use the following elementary consequence of weak convergence:
if u_t->u, y_t->g and nu{x:u.x=u.g}=0, then

    nu_t{x:u_t.x>=u_t.y_t}
                    ->nu{x:u.x>=u.g}.               (9)

Choose a ball strictly containing the compact support of nu.
Weak convergence makes the nu_t mass outside a slightly larger
ball tend to zero. On that ball the moving linear forms converge
uniformly. Sandwich their caps between the fixed limiting cap
with thresholds shifted by plus and minus delta, apply the open/
closed forms of Portmanteau, and then let delta decrease to zero.
The null-boundary assumption proves (9). In particular no relation
between a convergence rate and t is introduced.

Write F(y,u)=|T intersect {u.x>=u.y}|. It is jointly continuous
for y near g and |u|=1, by bounded convergence and the nullity of
hyperplane volume for T. Near the canonical unit normal u_i,
the cut at points near g has exactly one strictly positive vertex
margin a_i=u.(v_i-y) and d strictly negative vertex margins a_j.
Its exact volume is

    F(y,u)=V a_i^d/product_{j!=i}(a_i-a_j).            (10)

The denominators remain nonzero. This is a smooth function of
y and u in that neighborhood. At the canonical direction,

    D_y F(g,u_i)[v]=-kappa l_i(v).                    (11)

Both its first derivative and the local Taylor remainder are
uniform on a smaller compact normal neighborhood. Formula (10)
also proves this directly without assuming generic polytope-cap
regularity at arbitrary cuts.

## 4. Lower bound over ALL directions

Define x_t=g+t v_* with v_* from (4); this belongs to int T for
small t. We claim

    inf_{|u|=1} [F(x_t,u)+t nu_t(H(x_t,u))]
                         >=Gamma V+t pbar-o(t).      (12)

Here H(x,u) denotes {z:u.z>=u.x}. If (12) failed, take a sequence
t tending to zero and approximately minimizing directions u_t
violating it by a fixed positive multiple of t. The sphere is
compact, so pass to u_t->u. Positivity of the perturbing measure
and joint continuity of F show F(g,u)<=Gamma V. By the equality
classification in Section 1, u must be one canonical direction,
say u_i.

The uniform local expansion (10)-(11) gives

    F(x_t,u_t)=F(g,u_t)-t kappa l_i(v_*)+o(t)
             >=Gamma V-t kappa l_i(v_*)+o(t).         (13)

The nonnegative unperturbed excess F(g,u_t)-Gamma V is retained
in this inequality; no rate of convergence of the normals is
assumed. Equations (1) and (9) give the added cap mass p_i+o(1).
Combining with (13) gives

    F(x_t,u_t)+t nu_t(H(x_t,u_t))
       >=Gamma V+t[p_i-kappa l_i(v_*)]+o(t)
        =Gamma V+t pbar+o(t),

the required contradiction. Approximate minimizers suffice; no
attainment of the cap-normal infimum for atomic nu_t is assumed.
This proves the all-direction lower bound and hence that side of (2).

## 5. Matching upper bound and every maximizer's displacement

At any maximizing y_t, Section 2 gives |y_t-g|=O(t). For each
fixed canonical direction its moved cap therefore has mass

    Gamma V-kappa l_i(y_t-g)+t p_i+o(t).             (14)

The T-volume remainder is O(t^2), and the added-measure remainder
is t o(1) by (9). Depth is at most each of these cap masses, hence
at most their average. Since sum_i l_i=0, averaging (14) proves

    D_t<=Gamma V+t pbar+o(t).

Together with Section 4 this proves (2), and division by V+t
proves (3).

For (4), put w_t=(y_t-g)/t, which is bounded by Section 2.
The now known value (2) and each inequality (14) imply

    p_i-kappa l_i(w_t)-pbar>=-o(1).

These m quantities sum to zero exactly. Therefore each tends to
zero. The barycentric linear map is injective onto the zero-sum
subspace, so w_t->v_*. This holds for every maximizing selection,
even when the perturbed maximum is not unique at finite t.

The coefficient pbar is exactly the expected number of canonical
caps containing a nu-point, divided by m. Away from their boundary
planes the m margins sum to zero, so at least one and at most d
are positive. Hence the sharp first-order range is

    1/(d+1)<=lim_(t->0) (D_t-Gamma V)/t<=d/(d+1).

Both endpoints are attained by probability laws supported on the
corresponding open regions inside T (near a vertex for multiplicity
one, and near the relative interior of an opposite facet for
multiplicity d). This is only a first-order statement at a simplex,
not a finite-added-mass inequality.

## 6. The thin cone law and the projected source application

Take the standard simplex T=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d), d>=2, with
g=(1/m,...,1/m), and

    E_epsilon=conv(0,g+epsilon e_1,...,g+epsilon e_d),
    0<epsilon<1/m.

It is contained in T. Its relative volume is exactly

    e_epsilon=|E_epsilon|/V
              =epsilon^(d-1)(h+epsilon).            (15)

This follows from the determinant of epsilon I+g 1^T. Uniform
barycentrics on E_epsilon give

    X_epsilon=r g+epsilon(lambda_1,...,lambda_d),
    r=sum_{i=1}^d lambda_i.

The law of r has density d r^(d-1) on [0,1], since the sublevel
simplex sum lambda_i<=r has relative volume r^d. Thus the uniform
probabilities on E_epsilon converge weakly to this law on [0,g].
The limiting measure gives zero mass to every canonical plane:
they meet this segment only at r=1. Its canonical masses are

    (p_0,p_1,...,p_d)=(1,0,...,0).                   (16)

Consequently the derivative in (3) is

    [1/(d+1)-Gamma_d]/V <0.                          (17)

For strictness, the d+1 canonical caps cover T, and when d>=2
an open subset belongs to at least two of them. Their equal
volume fractions therefore satisfy (d+1)Gamma_d>1.

For a fixed positive integer N consider the projected mixed law

    rho_epsilon=N 1_T dx+1_Eepsilon dx.

Apply the theorem after division by N, with
t=|E_epsilon|/N and nu_t uniform on E_epsilon. It gives the EXACT
first-order maximum, in unnormalized and normalized form:

    max A_rho =N Gamma_d V+|E_epsilon|/(d+1)
                                      +o(|E_epsilon|),
    max depth_rho =Gamma_d+(e_epsilon/N)
                          [1/(d+1)-Gamma_d]+o(e_epsilon).       (18)

Every maximizing point satisfies

    y_epsilon=g-
      e_epsilon/[N m d h^(d-1)] (1,...,1)+o(e_epsilon).         (19)

In d=2 the coefficient is exactly 1/(4N). Thus the explicit
meeting point g-e_epsilon(1,1)/(4N) in
candidate 74ee0d47d99d3779
has precisely the true maximizing point's first-order displacement.
Equation (18) supplies an all-normal matching asymptotic, beyond
that note's finite-cover upper bound. This is an ordinary projected
measure conclusion, not an oblique mixed-depth lower bound.

### Every projected maximizer is interior to the thin fiber

The stronger geometric conclusion also follows for d>=2. Let

    theta=e_epsilon/[N m d h^(d-1)],
    y_epsilon=g-theta 1+r_epsilon,  r_epsilon=o(e_epsilon).

This remainder is uniform over all maximizing points: otherwise
a sequence of violating maximizing choices would contradict (19).
The vertex matrix of E_epsilon is

    B_epsilon=epsilon I+g 1^T,
    B_epsilon^(-1)=epsilon^(-1)
                         [I-g 1^T/(epsilon+h)].

As g=(1/m)1, the non-apex barycentric coordinates of a maximizing
point are

    B_epsilon^(-1)y_epsilon
      =[(1/m-theta)/(epsilon+h)]1+B_epsilon^(-1)r_epsilon.

The last term has norm o(e_epsilon/epsilon)=o(1), since
e_epsilon/epsilon=epsilon^(d-2)(h+epsilon) stays bounded for d>=2.
Every non-apex coordinate therefore tends to 1/d and is positive.
Their sum has deficit from one exactly

    [epsilon+d theta-sum_i r_epsilon,i]/(epsilon+h)>0

for sufficiently small epsilon. Indeed theta is a fixed positive
multiple of e_epsilon, whereas the error is o(e_epsilon). Hence
EVERY projected maximizing point is in int(E_epsilon).

For the actual convex source with N consecutive T fibers followed
by E_epsilon, all intermediate real fibers contain E_epsilon.
Thus its ordinary projected Gamma failure occurs even though every
projected deepest point is interior to every real fiber. This does
not convert projected ordinary depth into an oblique mixed-depth
statement. The d=1 thin family is excluded because its added mass
does not vanish as epsilon tends to zero.

## 7. Why the null-boundary hypothesis cannot simply be dropped

Let T=[0,1], V=1 and g=1/2. If nu_t=delta_g, then the maximum
unnormalized depth is exactly 1/2+t, attained at g. Both canonical
closed half-lines have limiting nu mass one.

Instead let nu_t=delta_(g+sqrt(t)), for 0<t<1/4. The weak limit
is the same delta_g, but the maximum is exactly (1+t)/2, attained
at y=(1+t)/2 below the atom. The two cap masses there are y and
1-y+t. At the atom the right cap has mass 1/2-sqrt(t)+t, and
above it the right cap has even less; no point improves the value.

The derivatives are 1 and 1/2 despite the same weak limiting law.
Thus weak convergence alone, when the limit charges canonical
hyperplanes, does not determine the derivative from that limit.
Assumption (1) is a substantive hypothesis of the theorem.

## 8. Exact algebra checks

../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_ordinary_simplex_depth_first_variation.py passes 88 exact
checks under work/math-venv/bin/python: the affine canonical games,
the thin-simplex determinant and tails, the first coefficients of
the actual moving canonical caps, and soluble interval cases.
The compactness, all-normal lower bound and moving-cap weak-limit
arguments are proved above; no finite direction screen replaces them.
